teaching.explanationEs: Avisa primero de que es un idiom y luego da el significado en una frase corta.

teaching.explanationEs: Lost in translation: sentido que se pierde. Talk down to: hablar a alguien como si supiera menos; evítalo al aclarar.

prompt.es: Elige la mejor explicación sencilla de «the ball is in your court».

choices.text: It is not an idiom: it means that you must go to a tennis court soon.
It means the game is finished, so nobody has to do anything now.
It is an idiom: it means it is your turn to decide, so reply soon.

feedback.es: La mejor explicación avisa de que es un modismo y da el significado en una frase corta: te toca decidir y responder.

hint.es: Busca la explicación que avisa de que es un modismo y da el sentido real.

origin.text: A colleague from Japan has just read this line in an email: “The ball is in your court.” She writes to you: “I checked the dictionary, but I do not understand. Is it about tennis?”

prompt.es: Completa: «Perdona, eso es un modismo: no significa lo que dicen las palabras.»

feedback.es: Avisar de que es un idiom es el primer paso: así el otro sabe que no debe tomarlo al pie de la letra.

hint.es: Es la palabra para una expresión con sentido figurado.

origin.text: Your colleague looks confused when you say we are back to square one. You stop and explain: sorry, that is an ___; it does not mean what the words say, it means that we start again.

prompt.es: Ordena: «¿Tiene sentido para ti o prefieres que lo reformule?»

answer.text: Does that make sense to you or should I rephrase it

feedback.es: Does that make sense? comprueba la comprensión y should I rephrase it ofrece una segunda explicación.

hint.es: Empieza con Does that y termina con rephrase it.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué aclara la oradora tras usar un modismo.

choices.text: The project is paused for now, but it has not been cancelled.
The project goes on as planned, but the budget is reduced until March.
The project is on hold because the client wants a new offer.

feedback.es: Explica «on hold» como «we stop working on it for now» y añade que no está cancelado: está en pausa hasta marzo.

origin.audio: Sorry, I used an idiom in the meeting, and I saw some confused faces, and I wanted to be sure that everyone was following me. Let me put it simply: the project is on hold, which means that we stop working on it for now. It is not cancelled, and the client has not said no. We will look at it again in March, when the budget is clearer. Does that make sense? If not, I can write it down for you after the call.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada frase de aclaración con su función.

feedback.es: Cada frase cumple un paso distinto de la aclaración: reformular, comprobar, simplificar y detallar.

prompt.es: Elige la mejor explicación sencilla de «it would break the bank».

choices.text: It means it would cost exactly the money we have saved.
It means it would cost more money than we have.
It means it would cost less money than we expected.

feedback.es: Break the bank es costar más dinero del que se tiene; las otras opciones cambian el sentido: un préstamo no se menciona y cost less es lo contrario.

origin.text: A colleague from Brazil writes: “You said that the new stage would break the bank. What does it mean? I understood that it is something about a bank, but I do not see the connection.”

prompt.es: Elige qué explicación daría Mia a un colega extranjero sobre su segunda frase.

choices.text: It is an idiom: it means I am now very comfortable with my manager.
It is an idiom: it means I have decided to leave my job after this mistake.
It is an idiom: it means I might get into trouble at work soon.

feedback.es: En la reunión no hay lago ni hielo: la pista es el error y el jefe, así que es un modismo que significa estar en una posición arriesgada.

origin.text: At the lake, Mia said: “Careful, the ice is thin.” Later, in a team meeting, she told Leo: “After this mistake, I am on thin ice with my manager.” A colleague from abroad asks her what she meant.

prompt.es: Completa: «La semana pasada reveló el secreto del regalo.»

feedback.es: El verbo del modismo va en pasado porque la frase lleva last week; the beans no cambia.

origin.text: It was supposed to be a secret until Sunday. But last week she ___ the beans about the gift, and now everybody in the office knows what he is getting.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige por qué el colega pregunta «Is something cooking?».

choices.text: Because he thinks the phrase may really be about cooking.
Because he wants to know whether the team is planning something new.
Because he believes the plan is going very well.

feedback.es: El colega no conoce el modismo y busca un sentido literal («cooking»); la respuesta aclara que significa aplazarlo.

origin.audio: A colleague from abroad wrote to me: I read that our plan is on the back burner. Is something cooking? I smiled and answered in plain words: no, nobody is cooking. It means that we will work on the plan later, not now, because other tasks are more urgent this month.

prompt.es: Responde al mensaje de Sol: explica los dos modismos en inglés sencillo.

answer.text: Hi Sol, sorry about that. Those are idioms, and they do not mean what the words say. “Back to square one” means that we have to start again from the beginning. We made a plan, but it did not work, so we are at the start again. “Hit the nail on the head” means to say exactly the right thing. When Leo said the price was too high, he hit the nail on the head, because that was exactly the problem. In other words, the first idiom is about starting again and the second is about being exactly right. Let me put it simply: nobody is playing a game, and nobody is using a hammer. Does that make sense? If not, I can rephrase it or spell it out step by step. I will also write without idioms next time, so please tell me if any other phrase is unclear. I do not want anything to get lost in translation. Thank you for asking, and thanks for your patience!
accepted: Hi Sol, sorry about that. Those are idioms, and they do not mean what the words say. “Back to square one” means that we have to start again from the beginning. We made a plan, but it did not work, so we are at the start again. “Hit the nail on the head” means to say exactly the right thing. When Leo said the price was too high, he hit the nail on the head, because that was exactly the problem. In other words, the first idiom is about starting again and the second is about being exactly right. Let me put it simply: nobody is playing a game, and nobody is using a hammer. Does that make sense? If not, I can rephrase it or spell it out step by step. I will also write without idioms next time, so please tell me if any other phrase is unclear. I do not want anything to get lost in translation. Thank you for asking, and thanks for your patience!

Hello Sol, sorry, I used idioms. “Back to square one” means we must start again from the beginning, because our first plan did not work. “Hit the nail on the head” means to say exactly the right thing. Leo said the price was too high, and he was exactly right. In other words, the first idiom means we start again and the second means someone is correct. Is that clear? I can also spell it out step by step if you like, and next time I will use simple words, so please tell me if something is unclear. I do not want anything to get lost in translation, and I never want to talk down to you. Thanks for asking, and thank you for being so patient with our team. Do not hesitate to write to me again if another phrase is unclear to you.

feedback.es: La respuesta debe explicar los dos modismos en inglés sencillo, usar una fórmula de aclaración y comprobar que Sol entendió.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué opina Leo del comentario de Mia.

choices.text: He is slightly annoyed that she said aloud what he was about to say.
He agrees fully and likes the way she put it.
He is impressed but thinks she should have spoken before the meeting.

feedback.es: Leo dice que es exactamente lo que quería decir y que no encontraba las palabras: está de acuerdo y admira cómo lo dijo ella.

origin.audio: After the meeting, Leo said to Mia: you hit the nail on the head. That is exactly what I wanted to say, but I could not find the words. Mia laughed and answered that she had only said what everybody was thinking. Then a colleague from Brazil asked what the idiom meant, and Leo explained: it means that someone has said exactly the right thing.

prompt.es: Completa: «Déjame reformularlo: necesitamos tu respuesta para el viernes.»

feedback.es: Let me rephrase that es la fórmula para volver a decir lo mismo con otras palabras, más claras.

origin.text: I saw a confused look on her face after my long sentence, so I smiled and said: let me ___ that: we need your answer by Friday.

prompt.es: Elige la frase mejor escrita para un cliente extranjero.

choices.text: The offer is open, the ball is in your court and we are on the same page.
The offer is open; in a nutshell, it is a piece of cake to accept it.
The offer is open; in other words, you can accept it until Friday.

feedback.es: Es clara, da la fecha y usa in other words para simplificar; las otras acumulan modismos que el cliente dijo no entender.

origin.text: You are writing to a client who is learning English and who has told you that idioms are hard for him. You want to tell him that he can accept the offer until Friday.
